{"id": "18:1/q13", "question": "How do ʿiwaj and ʿawaj differ?", "turns_on": "Whether the kasra and fatḥa forms encode an abstract versus physical distinction; 20:107 challenges a strict division.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q13/p1", "position": "Kasra generally concerns immaterial or subtle crookedness, while fatḥa concerns visible physical crookedness.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites religion and a stick; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes roads, al-Qurṭubī thought and affairs, and al-Ālūsī reports the distinction. Al-Biqāʿī applies it to the Book's meanings. Al-Ālūsī tests 20:107's physical earth and reports a reply about subtle unevenness, though its 'you do not see' suggests sight; Ibn al-Sikkīt makes kasra broader."}, {"id": "18:1/q13/p2", "position": "They have no difference in meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports al-Marzūqī's choice in his commentary on al-Faṣīḥ."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q14", "question": "What does 'for it' refer to, and what does the preposition suggest?", "turns_on": "Which earlier masculine noun supplies the pronoun's antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q14/p1", "position": "It refers to the Book; 'for' emphatically denies any possible crookedness in it.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says this is the apparent antecedent. {"id": "18:1/q15", "question": "How are the no-crookedness clause and qayyiman constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether the apparent order is transposed, circumstantial, coordinated inside the relative clause, or completed by an omitted verb; whether an intervening clause can separate qayyiman from its owner.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q15/p1", "position": "The wording is transposed in sense: God sent down an upright Book and made no crookedness in it; qayyiman is circumstantial.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, grammarians quoted by al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās report this. Al-ʿAskarī says eloquence places the important first. Al-Rāghib counts it as ambiguity of word order. Al-Zarkashī says Rāzī's intrinsic-versus-extrinsic objection confuses syntactic order with order of truth; al-Wāḥidī calls this the linguists' and exegetes' view."}, {"id": "18:1/q15/p2", "position": "The clause follows 'sent down' in the relative clause; an implicit verb governs qayyiman, as though 'but made it upright'.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī avoids separating a circumstantial from its owner by relative-clause material. Abū Ḥayyān reports this; al-Zarkashī finds coordination within the relative clause most apparent and notes an answer that coordination avoids interruption. Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects this against context."}, {"id": "18:1/q15/p3", "position": "The no-crookedness clause and qayyiman are circumstantial descriptions of the Book in the stated order.", "reasons": "Al-Kirmānī and al-Aṣbahānī give sequential circumstantials; Ibn al-Munayyir says both clauses describe the same Book, an analysis earlier scholars also gave. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers it from context. Al-Zarkashī records a clause governed by 'sent down' and another as independent coordination, which he prefers because denial is absolute rather than limited to revelation. Qatāda supplies 'but made it upright'."}, {"id": "18:1/q15/p4", "position": "Qayyiman modifies the pronoun in lahu, as an emphatic stable or temporary circumstance.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān proposes this; al-Zarkashī reports a circumstantial of the pronoun. Ṭabāṭabāʾī records and rejects it on contextual grounds."}, {"id": "18:1/q15/p5", "position": "Qayyiman substitutes for the negated clause or for ʿiwajan.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports Ḥall al-ʿIqd's substitute for the clause, noting grammatical dispute. Al-Zarkashī finds substitution for ʿiwajan unclear, and says opposites cannot qualify one another."}, {"id": "18:1/q15/p6", "position": "The stated order is meaningful: denying intrinsic defect precedes describing the Book's benefit to others.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī rejects transposition as rationally impossible; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Zarkashī report it, and al-Zarkashī objects that this conflates syntax with temporal or logical priority."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q16", "question": "How is the hāʾ pronoun read in ʿabdihi and similar forms?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q16/p1", "position": "Before a silent consonant after kasra or silent yāʾ, it has kasra with no linking vowel, as in ʿabdihi.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says all readers follow this rule; before a vowel, prior fatḥa or ḍamma yields wāw-linking and prior kasra yāʾ-linking; before a sākin after other sounds it has ḍamma without linking. He notes Ibn Kathīr's linking after a sākin before a vowel and Ḥafṣ's exceptions at 18:63, 48:10 and 25:69."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q17", "question": "Why and how is a pause made after ʿiwajan?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q17/p1", "position": "Ḥafṣ pauses briefly without taking breath, separating qayyiman from ʿiwajan so uprightness cannot be mistaken as a description of crookedness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya also notes his pause at marqadnā, 36:52; Abū Ḥayyān calls a Companion codex's 'but made it upright' explanatory, not Qur'anic. {"id": "18:1/q18", "question": "Why is 'Book' placed after 'upon His servant'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q18/p1", "position": "Delaying the direct object lets the following no-crookedness clause attach immediately to 'Book'.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this word-order explanation."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q19", "question": "What questioners or event prompted the opening?", "turns_on": "The notes report both the Jewish objection and a delayed reply to Quraysh; they emphasize different aspects of the opening's occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q19/p1", "position": "Jewish questioners objected that Muhammad's Book came differently from the Torah's separately revealed sections.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports their objection."}, {"id": "18:1/q19/p2", "position": "After revelation paused, the opening answered Quraysh's questions about the Cave youths and rebuked their wish for the Prophet's failure.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya emphasizes their seeing blessing descend on him. Ibn al-Zamalkānī says the delayed answer reassured him that God had not withdrawn favor. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it consoles him and then turns from worldly adornment to the youths."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q20", "question": "What does qayyiman mean of the Book?", "turns_on": "Whether qayyiman primarily confirms intrinsic straightness, describes authority over scriptures, or denotes guidance of human affairs.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q20/p1", "position": "Upright, just, flawless, moderate, or balanced, confirming the denial of crookedness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as just; al-Ḍaḥḥāk adds wisdom with no error, corruption or contradiction, which al-Qurṭubī commends. Al-Kashshāf says the double assertion rules out subtle defects, and Abū Ḥayyān attributes its confirmatory force to Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports balance without excess or deficiency; Ibn Isḥāq says moderate."}, {"id": "18:1/q20/p2", "position": "It upholds, verifies, witnesses to, or abrogates earlier scriptures.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says it verifies other books; al-Thaʿlabī reports its authority and abrogation of their laws; al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī record variants including preserving and confirming them."}, {"id": "18:1/q20/p3", "position": "It orders people's interests through right belief, good action, laws, and welfare in both lives.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this in context and cites 46:30 and 30:43; al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān report people's laws and interests. Al-Qurṭubī also reports the Book as enduring proof."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q21", "question": "What larger purpose does the sūra's opening announce?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q21/p1", "position": "It confirms revelation and the Prophet's mission while warning rejecters and promising believers reward.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq says it answers deniers of prophethood; al-Wāḥidī says the ensuing verses rebuke Quraysh's claim that angels are God's daughters; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it confronts polytheists and their scriptural informants and denial of divine offspring. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says true belief and good action frame the sūra, with special rejection of divine child claims. İslâhî says warning and glad tidings are the Prophet's task and unbelief is no failure of Book or preaching."}, {"id": "18:1/q21/p2", "position": "It tests attachment to worldly beauty and uses stories to teach piety, faith, and accountability.", "reasons": "Asad points to the rich and poor men's parable. Ṭabāṭabāʾī identifies the Cave youths, Moses and companion, and Dhū al-Qarnayn as unusual narratives against association. Al-Biqāʿī says the Moses-Khiḍr story corrects Israelites' pride in answering Quraysh; the spirit question links al-Isrāʾ's unseen theme and Qur'an as greater spirit."}, {"id": "18:1/q21/p3", "position": "Its connected narratives repeated

{"id": "18:1/q22", "question": "How is al-Kahf's place among the sūras explained?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q22/p1", "position": "Its praise opening mirrors key divisions of the Qur'an and the sequence of praise-opened sūras.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it opens the Qur'an's second half with al-ḥamdu li-llāh, echoing al-Fātiḥa and the approximate fourth-quarter opening in 35:1. {"id": "18:1/q24", "question": "How many verses does al-Kahf contain?", "turns_on": "Regional verse-counting conventions.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q24/p1", "position": "110 in the Kufan count.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf gives 110; al-Ālūsī specifies the Kufan tradition."}, {"id": "18:1/q24/p2", "position": "111 in the Basran count.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the regional count."}, {"id": "18:1/q24/p3", "position": "106 in the Syrian count.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the regional count."}, {"id": "18:1/q24/p4", "position": "105 in the Hijazi count.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the regional count."}]}

{"id": "18:1/q26", "question": "What recitations or memorization of al-Kahf are commended?", "turns_on": "The reports specify different times, verse counts, benefits, and one explicitly weak chain.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q26/p1", "position": "Friday recitation brings light and forgiveness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar's report promises light from feet to sky until resurrection and forgiveness between Fridays; Abū Saʿīd's reports promise light between reader and Sacred House. {"id": "18:1/q33", "question": "What wider disciplines or structures are invoked to study the Book's arrangement?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q33/p1", "position": "Its composition, verse order, sūra links and rhetorical devices form an intentionally wise system.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī describes divine arrangement, eloquence and proofs; his Asrār al-Tanzīl studies how each sūra elaborates its predecessor, opening-to-purpose fit, beginnings and endings, interrelated verses, address shifts, metaphor, metonymy, wordplay, antithesis, concision and expansion. {"id": "18:1/q34", "question": "What rank is given to Muhammad and those who carry the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q34/p1", "position": "Muhammad is God's beloved, protected, unlettered Messenger, named in earlier scriptures.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf invokes blessings on him, his family, successors, Emigrants and Helpers, and describes him as supported by wisdom and named in Torah and Gospel."}, {"id": "18:1/q34/p2", "position": "The Qur'an's recipient is the best prophet and its bearers, reciters and teachers are especially honored.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī argues from its status as the greatest revealed Book to the excellence of its prophet and community; he cites Ibn ʿAbbās's report that the Prophet called its bearers the community's noblest."}]}

{"id": "18:32/q02", "question": "What does the command to strike a parable ask the Prophet to do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q02/p1", "position": "Recount the illustrative story of two men to the audience.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān glosses the imperative as recounting the story; Baghawī says it asks the audience to recall it."}]}

{"id": "18:32/q22", "question": "How does this parable connect with its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "The notes trace different contextual links: immediate social dispute, reported questions, sūrah theme, al-Ṣāffāt's companion, and other garden passages.", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q22/p1", "position": "It answers rich unbelievers who disdain poor believers and boast of worldly wealth or supporters.", "reasons": "Rāzī, Qurtubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, Biqāʿī and Study Quran relate it to the command to remain with poor believers and the opponents' demand for their expulsion; Biqāʿī cites 18:28–29. {"id": "18:32/q24", "question": "How is the parable read inwardly?", "turns_on": "The inward readings use different symbolic schemes: two spiritual trajectories or the struggle of self and heart.", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q24/p1", "position": "Two servants receive divine gentleness; one advances from good beginnings through character and pure states to self-annihilation in unity.", "reasons": "Qushayrī describes the successful servant's struggle and completion through spiritual stations."}, {"id": "18:32/q24/p2", "position": "The other servant neglects his beginning and falls back into habit, heedlessness and estrangement.", "reasons": "Qushayrī describes abandonment of the path followed by separation, expulsion and humiliation."}, {"id": "18:32/q24/p3", "position": "The two men signify an unbelieving self and believing heart, and garden features signify desires and human faculties.", "reasons": "Al-Nīsābūrī maps the gardens to desire and the world, grapes to lusts, palms to leadership, crops to animal pleasures and the river to faculties and senses; later fruit and boasting signify cravings and blameworthy traits, while overturned hands signify regret for a wasted life."}]}
{"id": "18:32/q25", "question": "What does wāw contribute when it coordinates items or clauses?", "turns_on": "The grammatical force of each coordinating particle: bare joining, succession, alternative or exclusion.", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q25/p1", "position": "It joins elements under a shared relation without itself specifying order, delay or alternative.", "reasons": "Sībawayh's passage example allows either order or simultaneous action; Jurjānī contrasts fa, thumma and aw. He says coordinated clauses also require a meaningful connection, as with Zayd and ʿAmr, while unrelated clauses become absurd."}, {"id": "18:32/q25/p2", "position": "Unlike wāw, fa sets the first event as the starting point.", "reasons": "Sībawayh illustrates passing Zayd then ʿAmr."}, {"id": "18:32/q25/p3", "position": "Unlike wāw, thumma marks two passages with the first as starting point.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says both remain coordinated under the preposition."}, {"id": "18:32/q25/p4", "position": "Unlike wāw, aw offers alternatives, affirming one rather than both.", "reasons": "Sībawayh explains how to deny both or specify which one is denied."}, {"id": "18:32/q25/p5", "position": "Unlike wāw, lā affirms the first coordinated noun and excludes the second.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says it clarifies which passage was meant."}]}
{"id": "18:32/q26", "question": "How do the parts of a compound simile relate to one another?", "turns_on": "Whether a comparison treats its images as defining conditions, subordinate descriptions, or parallel components.", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q26/p1", "position": "A valid comparison must preserve the defining features of the whole compared image.", "reasons": "Jurjānī says a generic red rose fails when the intended flower has white around its red center; his praise-and-pearl example compares the whole wasted act, not hanging alone, with wāw meaning 'with' because no parallel predicates exist."}, {"id": "18:32/q26/p2", "position": "One image in a compound simile can be subordinate to another, as a descriptive or circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Jurjānī uses gray hair in youth, a circumstantial wāw with Mars and Jupiter, falling stars as a description of night, and day calling at night's sides."}, {"id": "18:32/q26/p3", "position": "Some compound comparisons coordinate their components as equals on both sides.", "reasons": "Jurjānī treats Imruʾ al-Qays's paired dates as an exception, with explicit coordination in 'fresh and dry'; a plural subject can encompass distinct equal items."}]}
{"id": "18:32/q27", "question": "How are competing poetic depictions assessed?", "turns_on": "The cited poetic evidence compares natural eloquence, crafted imagery, fuller effects and reversal of an expectation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q27/p1", "position": "Al-Nābigha's opening powerfully depicts distress and sleepless night.", "reasons": "Khaṭṭābī reports praise that no poet began better; he explains the relieved chest through a shepherd settling camels, joining natural ease, eloquence and sweetness."}, {"id": "18:32/q27/p2", "position": "Imruʾ al-Qays surpasses al-Nābigha in crafted simile and inventive meaning.", "reasons": "Khaṭṭābī points to embodied night, darkness like colliding sea waves, stars tied motionless, and the reversal from longing for dawn to despair that any time can cure the pain; a report has al-Walīd stamp his foot and al-Shaʿbī recognize the excellence."}, {"id": "18:32/q27/p3", "position": "Poems on one subject can be ranked by achievement; al-Aʿshā's wine verse surpasses al-Akhṭal's.", "reasons": "Khaṭṭābī says a comparison decides whether one leads, falls short or equals another. Hishām reports al-Shaʿbī's judgment and al-Akhṭal's concession. Khaṭṭābī prefers the image of aroma curing congestion over one merely reaching a person with a cold."}, {"id": "18:32/q27/p4", "position": "A striking poetic contest may build an idea up before reversing or demolishing it.", "reasons": "Khaṭṭābī states the device; Ḥassān's verse for Jabala begins by seeming to disparage the wine cup he desired to renounce."}]}
{"id": "18:32/q28", "question": "Is Qurʾānic inimitability a matter of knowing its composition or being able to produce it?", "turns_on": "Whether knowing compositional rules suffices to reproduce the achievement; Bāqillānī argues that skill and capacity can fail despite knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q28/p1", "position": "It rests on an inability to produce Qurʾānic composition, even when rules are known.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī compares known meters, eloquence, weaving and archery with unequal execution; an exceptional verse or inability to copy an existing line shows knowledge and capacity can diverge."}, {"id": "18:32/q28/p2", "position": "It rests on the Messenger's privileged knowledge of composition.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī attributes this to opponents and objects that it cannot distinguish divine from prophetic authorship."}]}
{"id": "18:32/q29", "question": "What do reports say about multiple permitted recitations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:32/q29/p1", "position": "The Prophet affirmed differing recitations and permission expanded to seven aḥruf for the community's ease.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī reports Gabriel's successive commands at Adhāt Banī Ghifār, Ubayy's encounter with different Sūrat al-Naḥl recitations, the Prophet's affirmation and prayer against Ubayy's misgivings, and requests for forgiveness with a final intercession reserved for Judgment Day. {"id": "18:34/q02", "question": "What does ثمر denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the context of the gardens controls the word, or Arabic usage and its readings extend it to property, principal assets, or separate produce.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q02/p1", "position": "Abundant wealth or property of many kinds.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda include gold, silver, livestock, fruit, and other assets; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes money, gardens and fields and derives the metaphor from assets fruiting, citing al-Nābigha. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this via al-Ṣiḥāḥ and al-Qāmūs; Ālūsī rejects mere produce as ill fitting. Some take wealth additional to the gardens, supporting expenditure on cultivation. Ālūsī cites Ubayy's explanatory codex phrase, 'We gave him abundant wealth.'"}, {"id": "18:34/q02/p2", "position": "Gold and silver in particular.", "reasons": "Mujāhid repeatedly specifies precious metal/cash; some place it alongside the two gardens. A few sources call this a metaphor for wealth that increases; Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says garden fruit fits better in context."}, {"id": "18:34/q02/p3", "position": "Fruit or produce of the two gardens.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī prefers it from 18:32 and reader consensus; Zajjāj, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAlī point to the preceding gardens or expenditure. Al-Layth defines tree borne fruit. Al-Kāshifī includes grapes, dates and other fruits; Iṣlāḥī reads harvest time as a moment of intoxication by plenty. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says mention of fruit implies future yields from roots. The word is a collective/plural with several derivations from thamrah and thimār, including the light form. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Ubayy's codex as saying abundant fruit or wealth."}, {"id": "18:34/q02/p4", "position": "The productive stock, roots or fruit-bearing trees.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd distinguishes the principal or stock from its yield; Abū ʿAlī and Ṭabrisī tie this to the owner's spending on roots and the later affliction that uprooted them, comparing 68:20. Some readings distinguish stock from fruit."}, {"id": "18:34/q02/p5", "position": "Date fruit specifically.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr assigns date palms to the open form, against all wealth for the rounded form; Abū ʿAlī identifies dates among the garden produce; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows this reading."}, {"id": "18:34/q02/p6", "position": "Fruit owned independently of the garden land or trees.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says he owned fruit without the trees or land, adding to the total wealth; Ṭabrisī reports it as an alternative to palms bearing fruit."}, {"id": "18:34/q02/p7", "position": "The open and rounded forms can share the same sense.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports semantic equivalence and then gold/silver, varied wealth and productive principal as glosses; Ibn al-Anbārī allows thumar to signify either fruit or amassed wealth. Other reported distinctions oppose fruit from one's own trees to acquired fruit, or yield to rootstock. Bashīr's thamar includes children and slaves while thumur is fruit, reversing the common assignment."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q03", "question": "What Meccan reading transmission background is recorded?", "turns_on": "The transmitters' relationships and how widely Meccans adopted their readings.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q03/p1", "position": "Ibn Kathīr's Meccan reading followed Mujāhid, who received it through Ibn ʿAbbās from Ubayy.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid says Ibn Kathīr never differed from Mujāhid; Ḥumayd ibn Qays also read with Mujāhid without differing, and Meccans remained united on Ibn Kathīr."}, {"id": "18:34/q03/p2", "position": "Ibn Muḥayṣin had Arabic expertise and independent choice but lacked Ibn Kathīr's Meccan consensus.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid says he studied with Darbās, Ibn ʿAbbās's freedman, as did Ibn Kathīr; he also studied with Mujāhid, who praised his Arabic ability."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q04", "question": "Why is ownership singular after the mention of two men?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q04/p1", "position": "Only one of the two men possessed this fruit or wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says mention of both in the parable's setup suffices for the later singular; al-Naḥḥās reports his explanation."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q05", "question": "Who is the companion addressed by the garden owner?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣāḥib and a claim of more nafar exclude kinship, or whether a brother can be called a companion and nafar denotes servants.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q05/p1", "position": "The believer is his brother or fellow companion.", "reasons": "Muqātil and several exegetes say they were brothers; Damghānī notes ṣāḥib can denote brother. {"id": "18:34/q06", "question": "What does يحاوره mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q06/p1", "position": "They exchange and return speech in reciprocal conversation or debate.", "reasons": "Several derive muḥāwara from ḥāra, to return; Rāzī, Samīn and others compare 84:14–15, and Samīn quotes Imruʾ al-Qays. {"id": "18:34/q08", "question": "What were the men discussing?", "turns_on": "The text reports reciprocal speech without quoting the preceding exchange; sources reconstruct its topic from the parable and its continuation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q08/p1", "position": "They disputed faith and unbelief, including resurrection and gratitude.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī list this as a topic.
